items.title: Who's who in Yemen
items.sum: Yemen has two rival governments. The Houthis rule Sanaa and the north-west, where most Yemenis live; the internationally recognised government, led by an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council and backed by Saudi Arabia, holds the south and east from Aden.
items.detail:
The Houthis: The movement calls itself Ansar Allah. Its leader is Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in charge since 2004. Mahdi al-Mashat heads its Supreme Political Council in Sanaa. Muhammad Miftah has been acting prime minister there since an Israeli strike killed Ahmed al-Rahawi in August 2025, and Yusuf al-Madani has been chief of staff since October 2025. Yahya Saree is the military spokesman; Mohammed Abdulsalam is the chief negotiator, based in Muscat.

The government: Since April 2022 a Presidential Leadership Council has held the president's powers. Its chairman is Rashad al-Alimi. The other members are Tareq Saleh, Sultan al-Arada, Abdullah al-Alimi Bawazeer, Abu Zaraa al-Mahrami, Othman Mujalli, and, since 15 January 2026, Mahmoud al-Subaihi and Salem al-Khanbashi. Shaya al-Zindani has been prime minister since January 2026. The government sits in Aden; many of its leaders spend much of their time in Riyadh.

The STC: The Southern Transitional Council, founded in 2017 under Aidarous al-Zubaidi, wants a separate southern state and was backed by the UAE. After it seized Hadramawt and Al-Mahra in December 2025, the council removed al-Zubaidi and he left for the UAE. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC's dissolution on 9 January 2026; its spokesman in Abu Dhabi rejected that.

Islah: The Yemeni Congregation for Reform is a Sunni Islamist party founded in 1990, with Muslim Brotherhood roots and tribal backing. It is strong in Marib and Taiz. Al-Arada, the governor of Marib, is close to it.

The west coast: Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late president Ali Abdullah Saleh, leads the National Resistance, based on the Red Sea coast around Mocha until the Houthis took the town in September 2026. The Giants Brigades are southern, largely Salafi units formed with UAE support in 2015 and led by Abu Zaraa al-Mahrami.

The outside powers: Saudi Arabia has led the coalition against the Houthis since 2015 and is now the government's main backer. The UAE was its main partner and armed the southern forces; it said its last troops left Yemen on 2 January 2026.

AQAP: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, led by Saad bin Atef al-Awlaki since 2024, fights both sides and is active mainly in Abyan, Shabwa and Al-Bayda.

items.title: North and South: the two Yemens
items.sum: Until 1990 there were two Yemen states: a republic in the north and a Marxist state in the south. They united in 1990, fought a war in 1994, and many southerners have demanded their own state again since 2007.
items.detail:
Two histories: Britain took Aden in 1839 and ruled the south as a colony and protectorates. The north was ruled by Zaydi imams; it became a kingdom on the Ottomans' departure in 1918.

The north: An army revolt in September 1962 overthrew the imam and declared the Yemen Arab Republic, with its capital in Sanaa. A civil war followed until 1970, with Egypt backing the republicans and Saudi Arabia the royalists. Ali Abdullah Saleh became president in 1978.

The south: Britain left on 30 November 1967. The new state became the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen in 1970, a one-party Marxist state allied with the Soviet Union, with its capital in Aden. The two Yemens fought border wars in 1972 and 1979, and a short civil war inside the south's ruling party in January 1986 killed thousands.

Unification: As Soviet support ended, the two states merged on 22 May 1990 as the Republic of Yemen. Saleh became president and the south's leader, Ali Salem al-Beidh, vice-president.

The 1994 war: Power-sharing broke down. Fighting began in May 1994, al-Beidh declared a breakaway southern state on 21 May, and northern forces took Aden on 7 July. Al-Beidh went into exile; he died in January 2026.

The southern movement: Southerners complained of land seizures and of losing jobs in the army and state. From 2007 protests by retired southern officers grew into the Southern Movement, known as al-Hirak, which demands self-rule or independence. The STC grew out of it in 2017.

items.title: The Houthi movement
items.sum: The Houthis grew out of a Zaydi revival in Saada in the far north. Their founder was killed in 2004, and six rounds of war with the government by 2010 turned them into a hardened armed movement.
items.detail:
Zaydism: The Zaydis are a branch of Shia Islam found almost only in northern Yemen. Zaydi imams ruled parts of the north for about a thousand years, until the 1962 revolution. They make up roughly a third of Yemen's people.

The founder: In the early 1990s Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, from a family of religious scholars in Saada, helped lead the Believing Youth, a network of religious study groups. He sat in parliament from 1993 to 1997.

The slogan: After 2001 Hussein al-Houthi adopted the slogan "God is great, death to America, death to Israel, curse on the Jews, victory to Islam". It is still the movement's motto. Its ideology is opposed to the US and Israel, and it takes inspiration from Iran's revolution and from Hezbollah.

The Saada wars: In June 2004 President Saleh's government sent troops to arrest Hussein al-Houthi, who was killed in September 2004. Six rounds of fighting followed until February 2010. In the last round, from late 2009, Saudi Arabia fought the Houthis on its border.

The outcome: The wars ended without a winner. Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, Hussein's younger brother, took over the movement, and it came out with fighters, weapons and wide support in the north. From 2011 it called itself Ansar Allah, "Supporters of God".

items.title: From the uprising to the Houthi takeover
items.sum: The 2011 uprising forced Ali Abdullah Saleh out after 33 years. His successor Hadi led a national dialogue, but the Houthis, allied with Saleh, took Sanaa in 2014. The alliance ended when the Houthis killed Saleh in December 2017.
items.detail:
The uprising: Protests against Saleh began in January 2011. On 18 March gunmen killed about 50 protesters in Sanaa, and senior army officers broke with him. In June he was badly wounded in a bomb attack on his palace mosque.

Saleh's exit: Under a deal drawn up by the Gulf states and signed in Riyadh on 23 November 2011, Saleh handed power to his deputy, Abd Rabbuh Mansour Hadi, in return for immunity. Hadi was the only candidate in a vote on 21 February 2012.

The dialogue: A National Dialogue Conference met from March 2013 to January 2014 to plan a new constitution. In February 2014 a committee proposed a federal state of six regions. The Houthis and many southerners rejected it.

The takeover: The Houthis took Amran in July 2014 and entered Sanaa on 21 September 2014, with help from army units loyal to Saleh. In January 2015 they put Hadi under house arrest and he resigned. He escaped to Aden in February, withdrew his resignation, and fled to Saudi Arabia in March as the Houthis advanced south.

Saleh's end: Saleh and the Houthis ruled Sanaa together from 2016. On 2 December 2017 Saleh offered to talk with Saudi Arabia; fighting broke out in Sanaa and the Houthis killed him on 4 December. His nephew Tareq Saleh escaped and later formed the National Resistance.

items.title: The Saudi-led war and the peace talks
items.sum: A Saudi-led coalition went to war in March 2015 to restore Hadi. It retook the south but not Sanaa. A UN truce in April 2022 ended most fighting, and Saudi–Houthi talks produced a UN roadmap in December 2023 that was never signed.
items.detail:
The coalition: Saudi Arabia, the UAE and other Arab states began air strikes on 26 March 2015 (Operation Decisive Storm), and imposed a sea and air blockade. In April the UN Security Council put an arms embargo on the Houthis (Resolution 2216).

The south: Coalition-backed forces drove the Houthis out of Aden in July 2015. AQAP held Mukalla from April 2015 until UAE-backed forces took it back in April 2016.

Hodeidah: In June 2018 UAE-backed forces advanced on Hodeidah, the port for most of the north's food and fuel. Under the Stockholm Agreement of 13 December 2018 the sides agreed a ceasefire in Hodeidah, a prisoner exchange and talks on Taiz. A UN mission was set up to monitor the port.

Marib: From February 2021 the Houthis attacked Marib, the government's last stronghold in the north and the centre of its oil and gas. The city held, at a heavy cost on both sides.

The truce: A UN-brokered truce began on 2 April 2022. It allowed flights from Sanaa and fuel ships into Hodeidah. It formally expired on 2 October 2022, but large-scale fighting did not return until 2026.

The talks: Saudi envoys visited Sanaa in April 2023 and a Houthi delegation visited Riyadh in September 2023. On 23 December 2023 UN envoy Hans Grundberg said the sides had committed to a ceasefire and a roadmap including paid salaries and reopened roads, ports and the airport. The Red Sea crisis froze it.

The cost: The UN Development Programme estimated that by the end of 2021 about 377,000 people had died from the war, directly or from hunger and disease.

items.title: The Red Sea campaign
items.sum: After the war in Gaza began, the Houthis fired missiles and drones at Israel and attacked over 100 merchant ships. The US and Britain struck them from January 2024 until a US–Houthi deal in May 2025, and Israel struck Hodeidah and Sanaa.
items.detail:
The attacks: The Houthis fired their first missiles at Israel on 19 October 2023 and seized the car carrier Galaxy Leader on 19 November. They said they targeted ships linked to Israel, the US or Britain, but many had no clear link. Four ships were sunk: the Rubymar and Tutor in 2024, and the Magic Seas and Eternity C in July 2025. Several seafarers were killed.

The navies: The US launched Operation Prosperity Guardian on 18 December 2023 to escort ships. The EU's Operation Aspides, a defensive escort mission, began on 19 February 2024.

The strikes: US and British air strikes on Houthi targets began on 12 January 2024. The US stepped them up from 15 March 2025 (Operation Rough Rider). On 6 May 2025, in a deal mediated by Oman, the US stopped its strikes and the Houthis agreed to stop attacking US ships. The deal did not cover Israel.

Israel: After a Houthi drone killed a man in Tel Aviv on 19 July 2024, the Israeli Air Force struck the port of Hodeidah the next day, its first strike in Yemen. Israel later struck Hodeidah, Ras Isa, Sanaa airport and power stations. The IDF said its strike in Sanaa on 28 August 2025 killed the Houthi prime minister and other officials.

Since then: The Houthis halted their attacks when the Gaza ceasefire began on 10 October 2025. They fired at Israel again from 28 March 2026, during the Iran war, and in July 2026 declared a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping.

items.title: Iran's support and Houthi weapons
items.sum: Iran supplies the Houthis with missile and drone designs, parts and training, smuggled by sea and over land despite a UN arms embargo. The Houthis say they build their own weapons; UN experts found many are Iranian designs.
items.detail:
The relationship: The Houthis are part of the Iran-led "axis of resistance" with Hezbollah and armed groups in Iraq. UN experts reported in 2024 that the Houthis received weapons, training and money from Iran, Hezbollah and Iraqi groups. Iran says it gives only political support.

The arsenal: Houthi ballistic missiles such as the Burkan and Toufan, the Quds cruise missile and the Samad drones closely match Iranian models. They have also fired anti-ship missiles and used explosive boats. With these they have reached Riyadh, Jeddah and Israel, some 2,000 km away.

Local assembly: Many weapons arrive in parts and are assembled in Yemen. The Houthis also took the Yemeni army's stocks in 2014 and 2015.

The routes: Dhows carry weapons from Iranian ports across the Arabian Sea, either to Yemen's coast or to Somalia, then into Yemen. Parts also cross by land from Oman through Al-Mahra, and small boats bring them to the Red Sea coast near Hodeidah.

Interdictions: The US and its partners have seized many shipments. In January 2024 two US Navy SEALs died while boarding a dhow carrying Iranian missile parts off Somalia. In July 2025 the US Central Command said Tareq Saleh's forces had seized more than 750 tons of Iranian weapons bound for the Houthis, its largest such seizure.

items.title: The economy and aid
items.sum: Yemen has two central banks and two versions of the rial, worth very different amounts. Most state salaries in the north have gone unpaid for years, oil exports have stopped, and in 2026 the UN says 22 million people need aid.
items.detail:
Two central banks: In September 2016 the government moved the central bank from Sanaa to Aden. The Houthis kept running the old bank in Sanaa. Since then both claim to be the real one.

Two rials: In December 2019 the Houthis banned the new notes printed by the Aden bank. Old notes stay in use in the north and new ones in the south. In September 2026 a dollar bought about 530 rials in Sanaa but about 1,565 in Aden.

Salaries: Most state employees in Houthi areas have received little or no regular salary since 2016. Paying them was a main part of the UN roadmap.

Oil and ports: The government's oil exports stopped in October 2022, after Houthi drones hit the export terminals in Hadramawt and Shabwa. Hodeidah, with nearby Ras Isa and Salif, is the north's main port for food and fuel, and a UN mission has inspected ships bound there since 2016. Aden and Mukalla serve the south and east. The US listed the Houthis as a terrorist organisation again in March 2025, which made fuel imports to Houthi ports harder.

The aid crisis: The UN's 2026 plan, published in March, says 22.3 million people need aid, 18.3 million face acute hunger, more than 2.2 million young children are acutely malnourished and 5.2 million people are displaced. It asks for $2.16 billion to help 12 million people. The World Food Programme ended its work in Houthi areas in January 2026, after the Houthis detained UN staff and seized UN offices.

items.title: Bab el-Mandeb and the sea lanes
items.sum: The Bab el-Mandeb strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa is the southern gate of the Red Sea and the route to the Suez Canal. About 12 percent of the world's seaborne oil passed through it before the Houthi attacks.
items.detail:
Geography: The strait joins the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. It is about 32 km wide, between Yemen on one side and Djibouti and Eritrea on the other. The name means "Gate of Tears" in Arabic.

Perim: The small Yemeni island of Perim, called Mayun in Arabic, splits the strait into a narrow eastern channel of about 3 km and a western channel of about 26 km, which big ships use. Government forces held it until September 2026, when the Houthis took it.

The Red Sea islands: Zuqar and the Hanish islands lie further north, between Yemen and Eritrea. Eritrea seized Greater Hanish in December 1995; an international court awarded most of the islands to Yemen in 1998. Kamaran, off the port of Salif, is held by the Houthis.

Socotra: Yemen's largest island lies in the Arabian Sea off the Horn of Africa. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site for its rare plants. STC forces took it from the government in June 2020; the government said it took back all STC-held areas in January 2026.

The traffic: Ships between Europe and Asia pass the strait on the way to and from the Suez Canal. In 2023 about 8.7 million barrels of oil a day went through it. After the attacks began, many shipping lines sent their ships around Africa instead; in 2024 oil flows through the strait fell to about 4 million barrels a day, and Egypt's canal income fell sharply.
